Ex-Amsterdam to Asia/Mideast air cargo outlook positive
By Helen Hill

AMSTERDAM, May 29 (Reuter) - The ex-Amsterdam to Asia and Middle East markets are both stable and showing positive signs for the coming months although neither can be described as booming, a Reuters survey showed.
Japan especially was busy in the run up to the changes in its consumption tax which increased in April but since that time the Dutch-Japanese market has remained steady.
Pim De Goederen, cargo manager of Japan Airlines, said that the tax changes did not have as dramatic an impact as the Japanese airline may have expected.

In May, the Japanese market has been fairly busy especially in the perishables market. Plant cuttings are a big export from the Netherlands to Japan now but this market lasts only for one month from May until June, he said.
In addition, vegetables are a signficant export, especially peppers which make up around 90 percent of such exports via JAL. The flower bulb season then starts in July/August.

On the general cargo side, there has been an increase on last years levels but De Goederen described it as a 'reasonable growth' rather than a boom. Rates have also seen an increase on last year's levels and are remaining stable and at a reasonable level at 4.50 guilders per kilogram.

Nippon Cargo Airline's marketing manager, Tatsuya Katayama, also said that April was rather slow following the tax increases and that May is also a traditionally slow month in the Netherlands-Japan market.

Again perishables, especially peppers, are major exports with the Japanese all-cargo carrier. The cut flower market is not so strong as Japanese production of flowers is apparently booming because of favourable weather conditions, whereas the reverse is true of the Netherlands, with unfavourable weather conditions creating a dip in supply of flowers.

General cargo, on the other hand, is not terribly active from the Netherlands but German cargo, which is sent via Amsterdam, is strong, said Katayama. Machinery for replacing equipment in Japanese factories is the major stimulant for the Europe-Japanese market.

NCA operates five flights a week from the Netherlands, two of which also go via Milan. If cargo ex-Netherlands is not so strong, often Italy is better, so the two balance each other out he said. The fashion industry is the major export from Italy. Hong Kong, Taiwan and Singapore are all destinations which seem to be slightly busier than Japan.
Generally, Hong Kong is not quite as hectic as it was a few months ago.

Achim van der Graaff, cargo manager of Cathay Pacific and the new chairman of the Air Cargo Carriers Association of the Netherlands (ACAN) said he is confident that there is enough cargo for all the carriers at the moment even if it could not be described as booming.
The number of shipments has fallen but the weight of those shipments has increased. Van der Graaff feels this could be because agents are consolidating their consignments more.
The Hong Kong carrier has also noted there are fewer smaller shipments under 100 kilograms and ad hoc shipments to Hong Kong are slightly down.

Cathay is awaiting the opening of Hong Kong's new airport and the handover to the Chinese. This does not seem to be impacting the market, if the amount of block bookings for the coming months are considered, he added.
Rates to Hong Kong also appear to be stable, averaging at 2.90-3.00 guilders per kilogram.
Cathay Pacific increased its rates ex-Netherlands by three to four percent on all routes. Taiwan appears to be the destination that carriers are most optimistic on.

A China Airlines cargo spokesman said the Netherlands-Taiwan market is very' busy, although he admitted it is not down to Netherlands cargo itself as German, French, and British exports are boosting this market.
Machinery, chemicals and electrical equipment are exports from the Netherlands, he added. Only some 30 percent of traffic from the Netherlands is actually Dutch cargo, he said.

China Airlines operates six weekly MD-11 passenger flights from Amsterdam and a weekly freighter service to Taiwan which is operated with a Boeing 747-200 freighter, as well as services from Luxembourg.

EVA's general manager in the Netherlands, Han Lin, said the market is relatively busy currently but he is expecting June to pick-up even more. The forecast for the coming months between the Netherlands and Taiwan is very positive, with machinery' being the major export to Taiwan.

Rates to Taiwan are again stable at 2.55 guilders per kilogram. Singapore is slightly less at 2.60 guilders per kilogram on average. The Taiwanese carrier is considering the possibility' of introducing a rates increase for the the summer season but this is still under consideration.

EVA flies via Dubai to Taiwan from the Netherlands and this market is becoming increasingly competitive, said Lin. And the Netherlands-Middle East market is one that has seen some changes, as U.S. carrier, Polar Air entered the market with a twice-weekly freighter service via Dubai to India.
Middle East director of one of the lead forwarders in the Netherlands, MSAS, Tijn Middendrop, said the Middle East generally is not so active, with the exception of Dubai ex-Netherlands.

A major difference in the market is the result of the poultry' market which is usually a very healthy market from the Netherlands. Middendorp said shippers are buying both chickens and hatching eggs from local markets.
Dutch hatching eggs are in short supply and relatively expensive at the moment, he added, so the Middle East buyers purchase more from the U.S. or eastern Europe.
Dubai more than any other Middle Eastern destination is active, he said.
General cargo, including computers, offshore equipment and machinery' are exported from the Netherlands.
However, there is more capacity going to Dubai, and rates are under pressure, added Middendorp. Polar Air, EVA Air, Emirates, as well as Lufthansa and KLM are all major players in the market.
Several industry sources said rates to Dubai range from 1.80 to as low as 1.50 guilders per kilogram in this market.

Bahrain is a better destination rates wise said Middendorp because few carriers operate there and the yield is firmer. If capacity is short from Amsterdam, forwarders do use DHL which operates to Bahrain from Brussels.

Abu Dhabi was described as stable and relatively active by the China Airlines spokesman. But the rate to this destination does seem to be on the decline. --Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+5017
